note: 50 mixed-form items across the chapter's concepts. Difficulty 17 Easy / 17 Medium / 16 Hard.

items.stem: Reproduction involving only one parent is called
items.explanation: Asexual reproduction needs a single parent and the offspring are genetically almost identical to it.

options.why: Sexual reproduction involves two parents and the fusion of gametes.
Pollination is one step within sexual reproduction in flowers.
Fertilisation is the fusion of two gametes, so it needs both.

items.stem: Amoeba reproduces by
items.explanation: Amoeba divides into two daughter cells by binary fission.

options.why: Budding is seen in yeast and Hydra, not Amoeba.
Spore formation occurs in Rhizopus and ferns.
Vegetative propagation occurs in plants.

items.stem: Hydra reproduces asexually by
items.explanation: A bud develops on the parent body, grows and then detaches as a new individual.

options.why: Hydra is multicellular and does not split into two equal halves.
Hydra does not produce spores.
Layering is an artificial method used with plants.

items.stem: Fertilisation in human beings normally takes place in the
items.explanation: The sperm meets the egg in the oviduct, or fallopian tube, and the zygote then travels to the uterus.

options.why: The uterus is where the embryo implants and develops, after fertilisation.
The ovary releases the egg but is not where fusion happens.
The vagina receives the sperm but fertilisation occurs higher up.

items.stem: The transfer of pollen from the anther of one flower to the stigma of another flower of the same species is called
items.explanation: Transfer between two different flowers is cross-pollination; within the same flower it is self-pollination.

options.why: Self-pollination occurs within the same flower or the same plant.
Fertilisation is the later fusion of the male and female gametes.
Germination is the sprouting of a seed.

items.stem: A gardener wants plants identical to a prize rose. The best method is
items.explanation: Vegetative propagation produces genetically identical offspring, so the desired variety is preserved exactly.

options.why: Seeds come from sexual reproduction and vary from the parent.
Cross-pollination introduces variation from another plant.
Roses do not reproduce by spores.

items.stem: Menstruation occurs when
items.explanation: If the released egg is not fertilised, the thickened lining of the uterus is shed along with blood.

options.why: A fertilised egg implants and the lining is retained to nourish it.
That describes menopause, not the monthly cycle.
Puberty is when the cycle starts, not the cause of each occurrence.

items.stem: Variation among offspring arises chiefly because DNA copying is
items.explanation: Copying is remarkably accurate but not perfect, and the small differences that survive are the source of variation.

options.why: If copying were random the offspring would not resemble the parent at all.
Identical copying would produce no variation whatever.

options.text: carried out only in sexual reproduction
options.why: DNA is copied in both kinds of reproduction.

items.stem: Reproduction is essential for a species rather than for an individual because
items.explanation: An individual survives without reproducing, but without it the species cannot continue and cannot accumulate variation.

options.text: it maintains the species over generations
it keeps the individual alive longer
options.why: Reproduction does not extend an individual's own life.

options.text: it supplies energy to the individual
options.why: Energy comes from nutrition and respiration.

options.text: it removes waste from the body
options.why: Waste removal is the work of excretion.

items.stem: The main advantage of sexual over asexual reproduction is that it
items.explanation: Combining DNA from two parents produces much greater variation, which helps a species survive changing conditions.

options.text: is faster and needs less energy
options.why: Asexual reproduction is the faster and cheaper of the two.
That is a feature of asexual reproduction.
Asexual reproduction often produces far more offspring.

items.stem: What is regeneration? Name one organism that shows it.
items.answer: Regeneration is the ability of an organism to grow back a lost body part, or for a fragment to develop into a complete organism. Planaria and Hydra both show it.

items.stem: How does Rhizopus reproduce asexually?
items.answer: By spore formation. Erect hyphae bear round sporangia containing many spores, and when a sporangium bursts the spores are dispersed and each can grow into a new fungus on a suitable surface.

items.stem: Why are the testes located outside the abdominal cavity?
items.answer: Sperm formation requires a temperature a few degrees lower than the normal body temperature, and the scrotum outside the body provides it.

items.stem: How does multiple fission differ from binary fission?
items.answer: In binary fission the parent divides into two daughter cells, as in Amoeba. In multiple fission the parent divides simultaneously into many daughter cells, as in Plasmodium, which allows very rapid increase in numbers.

items.stem: Give two advantages of vegetative propagation.
items.answer: The offspring are genetically identical to the parent, so a desirable variety such as a particular mango or banana is preserved exactly. It is also faster than growing from seed, and it lets plants that produce few or no viable seeds be multiplied at all.

items.stem: Name the male and female reproductive parts of a flower.
items.answer: The male part is the stamen, made of the anther which produces pollen and the filament which supports it. The female part is the carpel or pistil, made of the stigma, the style and the ovary containing the ovules.

items.stem: Why is a barrier method of contraception preferred where infection is a concern?
items.answer: A barrier method physically prevents the sperm from reaching the egg and at the same time prevents direct contact, so it also reduces the transmission of sexually transmitted infections. Hormonal and surgical methods prevent pregnancy but give no protection against infection.

items.stem: Why is a moderate rate of variation better for a species than either none or a very high rate?
items.answer: With no variation, every individual is equally vulnerable and a single change in conditions could destroy the whole population. With very high variation, most changes would be harmful and the basic design of the organism would not be preserved. A moderate rate keeps the successful design while supplying enough differences for some individuals to survive a change.

items.stem: Describe four methods of asexual reproduction with one example of each.
items.answer: Fission, in which a single-celled parent divides into daughter cells. Binary fission gives two, as in Amoeba and Leishmania, while multiple fission gives many at once, as in Plasmodium. Budding, in which a small outgrowth appears on the parent, develops into a miniature individual and then detaches, as in yeast and Hydra. Fragmentation, in which a simple multicellular body breaks into pieces on maturing and each piece grows into a new individual, as in Spirogyra. Regeneration, in which a fragment of an organism develops into a complete one through specialised cells, as in Planaria. Spore formation, in which the parent produces many thick-walled spores that survive harsh conditions and germinate when conditions improve, as in Rhizopus. In every case a single parent is involved and the offspring closely resemble it.

items.stem: Describe the structure of a flower, naming its four parts and the role of each.
items.answer: A typical flower has four whorls attached to the receptacle. The calyx is the outermost whorl of sepals, usually green, which protect the flower while it is a bud. The corolla is the whorl of petals, often coloured and scented, which attract insects and other pollinators. The androecium is the male whorl, made of stamens, each consisting of an anther that produces pollen grains and a filament that holds it up. The gynoecium or carpel is the female whorl, made of the ovary containing one or more ovules, the style, and the stigma at the top which receives the pollen. A flower with both stamens and carpel is bisexual, as in hibiscus, while one with only one of them is unisexual, as in papaya and watermelon.

items.stem: Trace the events from pollination to seed formation in a flowering plant.
items.answer: Pollination occurs when a pollen grain lands on the stigma, carried there by wind, water or an animal. The pollen grain then germinates and grows a pollen tube down through the style towards the ovary. The tube carries the male gamete and delivers it into the ovule, where it fuses with the female gamete; this fusion is fertilisation and produces a zygote. The zygote divides repeatedly to form the embryo. Meanwhile the ovule develops a tough coat and becomes the seed, which contains the embryo and a store of food. The ovary around it grows and becomes the fruit, which protects the seeds and often assists their dispersal. The other parts of the flower, the sepals, petals, stamens, style and stigma, wither and fall away once they have done their work. When a seed reaches a suitable place with water, air and a suitable temperature, the embryo grows and germination produces a new plant.

items.stem: Describe the human female reproductive system and the changes that follow fertilisation.
items.answer: The system consists of a pair of ovaries, a pair of oviducts or fallopian tubes, the uterus and the vagina. The ovaries produce the egg cells and also secrete oestrogen. A single egg is usually released every month from one ovary, and it is drawn into the funnel-shaped opening of the oviduct. If sperm are present, fertilisation takes place in the oviduct and a zygote is formed. The zygote divides as it travels down the oviduct and reaches the uterus as a ball of cells, where it implants in the thickened lining. The lining develops into the placenta, a disc-shaped tissue with villi on the embryo's side, which brings the mother's blood and the embryo's blood close together so that glucose and oxygen can pass to the embryo and its wastes can pass back. The embryo develops in the uterus for about nine months, and the child is delivered by the rhythmic contraction of the uterine muscles. If fertilisation does not occur, the lining breaks down and is shed as the monthly menstrual flow.

items.stem: What changes mark puberty, and why do they occur at that stage?
items.answer: Puberty is the period during which the body becomes capable of reproduction, usually beginning between about ten and thirteen years of age. Changes common to both sexes include a growth spurt, the appearance of hair in the armpits and genital region, thinner and oilier skin with pimples, and a new awareness of the opposite sex. In boys the voice deepens as the larynx enlarges, facial hair appears, and the chest and shoulders broaden. In girls the breasts develop, the hips widen, and the menstrual cycle begins. These changes occur at this stage because the body must first complete enough of its general growth to support reproduction, and because the sex hormones, testosterone from the testes and oestrogen from the ovaries, begin to be secreted in quantity under the control of the pituitary gland. Reproduction is a demanding process, so the body does not become capable of it until it has the maturity to sustain it.

items.stem: Explain why sexual reproduction produces more variation than asexual reproduction.
items.answer: Three separate mechanisms contribute, and only the first is available to an asexual organism. First, DNA copying is never perfectly accurate, so small differences arise whenever cells divide; this happens in both kinds of reproduction and accounts for the slight variation among asexually produced offspring. Second, sexual reproduction combines DNA from two different individuals. The offspring receives one set of chromosomes from each parent, so it carries a combination that existed in neither parent alone, and the number of possible combinations is enormous. Third, when gametes are formed the two sets of chromosomes are separated and reshuffled, so each gamete carries a different mixture of the parent's own inherited material, and no two gametes from the same individual are alike. Because these mechanisms multiply together, the variation produced sexually is on a quite different scale from the copying errors available asexually. This is why asexually reproducing populations are nearly uniform and vulnerable to a single change in conditions, while sexually reproducing populations contain many differences and are far more likely to include individuals able to survive such a change.

items.stem: Explain why DNA copying is central to reproduction, and what happens if it goes seriously wrong.
items.answer: The most basic event in reproduction is the making of a copy of the DNA, because DNA carries the information for the design of the body. When a cell divides, each daughter cell must receive a complete copy, so the DNA is copied first and then the cellular apparatus is divided. The copies are made by the cell's own biochemical machinery, and since that machinery is not perfect, the copies are similar to the original but not always identical. These small differences are the raw material of variation and hence of evolution, so imperfect copying is not merely a fault but the mechanism by which populations can change. If the copying goes seriously wrong the consequences depend on the degree. A small error may have no effect at all, since much DNA does not specify anything critical, or it may produce a variation that happens to be useful. A larger error may produce a variation that the individual cannot survive, so that the newly made cell dies and no offspring results. Errors in the DNA of a body cell rather than a gamete may make that cell divide uncontrollably, which is the origin of cancer. So the accuracy of copying must be high enough to preserve the design and low enough to allow variation, and the observed rate reflects that balance.

items.stem: Discuss the reasons for family planning and the kinds of method available.
items.answer: Reproductive health means the total physical and social wellbeing associated with reproduction, and family planning is part of it. The reasons for planning are several. The health of the mother and child is better when pregnancies are spaced and when the mother is neither too young nor too old. A family can support and educate children better when their number matches its means. At the level of the population, a rapidly rising number of people places pressure on land, water, food, housing and employment, so planning affects the standard of living of everyone. The methods fall into four kinds. Barrier methods, such as the condom, physically prevent the sperm from reaching the egg, and they have the additional advantage of reducing the spread of sexually transmitted infections. Chemical or hormonal methods, such as oral pills, alter the hormone balance so that eggs are not released; they are effective but can have side effects and give no protection against infection. Intra-uterine devices placed in the uterus prevent implantation. Surgical methods, in which the vas deferens or the fallopian tubes are blocked, are effective and permanent and are chosen when a couple wants no further children. A method should be chosen with medical advice, since the right one depends on health, age and circumstances. It must also be said that these methods should never be used to determine the sex of a child, since selective abortion has already severely distorted the sex ratio in parts of the country and is prohibited by law.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Offspring produced asexually closely resemble the parent. Reason (R): They receive DNA from a single parent. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and receiving DNA from only one source is exactly why the resemblance is so close.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: A single DNA source is precisely why there is so little difference.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Asexual reproduction genuinely involves one parent only.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: Asexually produced offspring are nearly identical to the parent.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Plants grown by vegetative propagation vary widely from the parent. Reason (R): Vegetative propagation involves no fusion of gametes. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: The reason is true and is precisely what defeats the assertion: with no fusion of gametes the offspring are genetically identical.

options.text: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: No gamete fusion means no new combination, so no wide variation.

options.text: Both A and R are false
options.why: Vegetative propagation genuinely involves no gametes.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: The whole value of the method is that the offspring are identical.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Sexual reproduction is more efficient than asexual reproduction. Reason (R): Sexual reproduction produces greater variation. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: The reason is true but the assertion is false: sexual reproduction is slower and needs two parents, so it is less efficient while being more advantageous for survival.

options.text: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: Variation is an advantage for the species, not a gain in efficiency.

options.text: Both A and R are false
options.why: Sexual reproduction genuinely does produce greater variation.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Asexual reproduction is faster, cheaper and needs only one parent.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Menstruation means that no egg was released that month. Reason (R): The uterine lining is shed when the egg is not fertilised. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: The reason is true but the assertion is false: an egg is released and simply is not fertilised, so shedding indicates the absence of fertilisation, not of ovulation.

options.text: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: The egg is released; it is fertilisation that did not occur.

options.text: Both A and R are false
options.why: The lining is genuinely shed when fertilisation does not occur.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Ovulation precedes menstruation in a normal cycle.

items.stem: State whether true or false: yeast reproduces by budding.
items.explanation: A small bud grows on the parent cell, enlarges and then separates as a new yeast cell.

options.why: Budding is the characteristic method of asexual reproduction in yeast.

items.stem: State whether true or false: an individual organism dies if it does not reproduce.
items.explanation: Reproduction is essential for the species to continue, but an individual can live a full life without it.

options.why: Reproduction maintains the species, not the life of the individual.

items.stem: State whether true or false: pollination and fertilisation are the same event.
items.explanation: Pollination is the transfer of pollen to the stigma; fertilisation is the later fusion of gametes inside the ovule.

options.why: Pollination only delivers the pollen; fusion happens afterwards in the ovule.

items.stem: State whether true or false: regeneration is the same as reproduction.
items.explanation: Regeneration repairs or regrows a part and can produce a new individual in simple organisms, but it is not the normal means by which a species multiplies.

options.why: Regeneration is carried out by specialised cells and is not the usual way the species reproduces.

items.stem: The division of Amoeba into two daughter cells is called ___________ fission.
items.answer: binary

items.stem: The part of a flower that receives the pollen grain is the ___________.
items.answer: stigma

items.stem: The tissue that connects the embryo to the mother's uterine wall is the ___________.
items.answer: placenta

items.stem: The tube that carries sperm from the testis is called the vas ___________.
items.answer: deferens

items.stem: Explain why reproduction is important, and compare asexual and sexual reproduction under four headings.
items.answer: Reproduction is important not for the individual, who survives perfectly well without it, but for the species. It produces the next generation so the species continues after individuals die, it maintains the number of the population, and above all it passes on the DNA in which the body's design is encoded, together with the small variations that allow the species to change as conditions change. Comparing the two kinds: number of parents, asexual needs one while sexual needs two. Gametes, asexual involves none while sexual involves the fusion of a male and a female gamete. Variation, asexual produces offspring nearly identical to the parent, the only differences coming from copying errors, while sexual produces much greater variation because DNA from two individuals is combined and reshuffled. Speed and cost, asexual is rapid and requires little energy, so numbers can rise very fast, while sexual is slower and requires finding a mate. The consequence is that asexual reproduction suits a stable environment, where a design already proved successful should simply be repeated, while sexual reproduction suits a changing one, where a population containing many differences is more likely to include individuals that survive the change.

items.stem: Describe natural and artificial methods of vegetative propagation, and assess their usefulness.
items.answer: In natural vegetative propagation, new plants arise from the roots, stems, leaves or buds of the parent. The eyes on a potato tuber, the buds on a ginger rhizome, the runners of grass and the leaf notches of Bryophyllum all produce complete new plants. Artificial methods are those a gardener uses deliberately. In cutting, a piece of stem with a few buds is planted and develops roots, as with rose and sugarcane. In layering, a branch is bent down and part of it covered with soil until roots form, after which it is cut from the parent, as with jasmine. In grafting, a shoot of the desired variety, the scion, is joined to the rooted stem of a hardier plant, the stock, so that the fruit is of the chosen variety while the roots are strong, as with mango and apple. In tissue culture, a few cells from the growing tip are grown on a nutrient medium into a mass called a callus, which is then transferred to a hormone medium where it differentiates into plantlets, allowing thousands of identical plants from one parent. The usefulness is threefold. The offspring are genetically identical, so a prized variety is preserved exactly rather than varying as seedlings would. Plants that produce few or no viable seeds, such as banana, orange, rose and jasmine, can be multiplied at all. And flowering and fruiting come earlier than from seed. The drawback is the other side of the same coin: because every plant is identical, a disease that affects one affects the whole crop, and no variation is generated for the future.

items.stem: Explain why sexual reproduction, despite being slower and costlier, is so widespread.
items.answer: Sexual reproduction is expensive. It requires two parents, so an individual must find a mate, which costs time, energy and often risk. Only half of each parent's DNA passes to the offspring. The process is slower than simple division, and many organisms invest heavily in courtship, gametes and the care of the young. On the face of it an asexual organism, which can simply divide and does so rapidly, ought to outcompete it. The answer lies in variation. Asexual offspring differ from the parent only by copying errors, so an asexual population is close to uniform. If conditions change, through a new disease, a shift in climate or the arrival of a predator, then what harms one individual harms nearly all of them, and the population can be destroyed entirely. Sexual reproduction, by combining DNA from two individuals and reshuffling the chromosomes when gametes are formed, generates variation on a far larger scale. A sexually reproducing population therefore contains many different combinations, and when conditions change some individuals are likely to possess a combination that copes. Those survive and reproduce, and the population persists in an altered form. The advantage is thus not to the individual but to the lineage over generations, and it is realised only when the environment changes. This also explains the observed pattern in nature: many organisms use both, reproducing asexually while conditions are favourable and switching to sexual reproduction when they deteriorate, which takes the speed of one method and the insurance of the other.

items.stem: What is meant by reproductive health, and why does it need attention at both the individual and the social level?
items.answer: Reproductive health means the complete physical and social wellbeing of a person in all matters relating to reproduction, and not merely the absence of disease. At the individual level it covers several things. It covers accurate knowledge, since much harm comes from ignorance and from myths at the age of puberty. It covers the prevention and treatment of sexually transmitted infections such as gonorrhoea, syphilis and HIV-AIDS, for which a barrier method offers protection where hormonal and surgical methods do not. It covers the health of mother and child, which is better when pregnancies are spaced, when the mother is neither very young nor very old, and when medical care is available during pregnancy and delivery. It covers the freedom to decide whether and when to have children, for which reliable methods must be available together with medical advice on choosing among them. At the social level the matter goes further. The size and growth rate of a population determine the pressure on land, water, food, housing, schooling and employment, so decisions taken privately have public consequences, which is why family planning is a matter of national policy and not only of personal choice. Social attitudes matter too, since the stigma attached to discussing these subjects is itself a barrier to the knowledge that protects people. One social problem deserves separate mention. Techniques intended for detecting disorders in an unborn child have been widely misused to determine sex, followed by the abortion of female foetuses. This has already distorted the sex ratio severely in parts of the country, with consequences that will last generations, and it is for this reason that prenatal sex determination is prohibited by law. Reproductive health therefore requires medical provision, education and legal protection together, and none of the three is sufficient alone.

items.stem: One bacterium divides by binary fission every 20 minutes. How many bacteria are present after one hour?
items.answer: One hour contains three periods of 20 minutes, so three divisions occur. The number doubles each time: 1 becomes 2, then 4, then 8. So there are 8 bacteria after one hour.

items.stem: A bacterium divides every 30 minutes. Starting from one cell, find the number after 4 hours.
items.answer: Four hours contains 8 periods of 30 minutes, so 8 divisions occur. The number is 2 to the power 8, which is 256 bacteria. This geometric growth explains how an infection can become serious within hours, and why the doubling time rather than the current number is the figure to watch.

items.stem: If one egg is released every 28 days from about age 13 to about age 48, estimate the number released in a lifetime and comment.
items.answer: The reproductive span is about 48 minus 13, which is 35 years. Each year contains about 365 divided by 28, which is roughly 13 cycles. So the total is about 35 times 13, which is approximately 455 eggs. The comment worth making is how few this is compared with the number of sperm produced, which runs to many millions per day, and how few again compared with the number of eggs present in the ovary at birth, which is of the order of a million. The great majority never mature. The estimate is also rough, since cycles are interrupted by pregnancy and are irregular at the beginning and end of the span, so the figure should be treated as an order of magnitude rather than a precise count.

items.stem: Match each organism in Column I with its method of asexual reproduction in Column II. Column I: (a) Amoeba, (b) Hydra, (c) Rhizopus, (d) Planaria. Column II: (i) spore formation, (ii) regeneration, (iii) binary fission, (iv) budding.
items.answer: (a) Amoeba - (iii) binary fission. (b) Hydra - (iv) budding. (c) Rhizopus - (i) spore formation. (d) Planaria - (ii) regeneration.

items.stem: Match each flower part in Column I with its function in Column II. Column I: (a) anther, (b) stigma, (c) ovary, (d) petal. Column II: (i) attracts pollinators, (ii) receives pollen, (iii) contains ovules, (iv) produces pollen.
items.answer: (a) anther - (iv) produces pollen. (b) stigma - (ii) receives pollen. (c) ovary - (iii) contains ovules and later becomes the fruit. (d) petal - (i) attracts pollinators.

items.stem: Draw a labelled longitudinal section of a flower and mark the path of the pollen tube.
items.answer: Draw a vertical section through a flower on its receptacle. At the outside and lowest, draw and label the sepals forming the calyx. Above them draw and label the petals forming the corolla. Inside, draw two or more stamens, labelling the anther at the top of each and the filament beneath it. In the centre draw the carpel: the swollen ovary at the base containing one or more ovules, each labelled, then the narrow style rising from it, then the stigma at the top. Now draw a pollen grain resting on the stigma and label it. From it, draw a fine tube growing downwards through the style and entering an ovule, and label it pollen tube. Mark an arrow along the tube showing the direction of travel of the male gamete, and mark the point of fusion inside the ovule, labelling it fertilisation. Annotate the diagram with what each part becomes afterwards: the ovule becomes the seed, the ovary becomes the fruit, and the sepals, petals, stamens, style and stigma wither and fall. Add a note distinguishing pollination, the arrival of the grain on the stigma, from fertilisation, the fusion inside the ovule.

items.stem: Draw and label the human female reproductive system, annotating where each stage of early development occurs.
items.answer: Draw the uterus as a pear-shaped organ narrowing to the cervix below and opening into the vagina. From the upper corners of the uterus draw the two oviducts curving outwards and ending in funnel-shaped openings. Near each funnel draw an ovary. Label the ovaries, the funnel-shaped openings, the oviducts or fallopian tubes, the uterus with its thick muscular wall and inner lining, the cervix and the vagina. Now annotate each stage in sequence. At an ovary, mark release of one egg each month, and note that the ovary also secretes oestrogen. At the funnel, mark the egg is drawn into the oviduct. Partway along the oviduct, mark fertilisation occurs here if sperm are present. Along the rest of the oviduct, mark the zygote divides as it travels. At the uterine lining, mark implantation, and draw the embryo attached to the wall through a disc-shaped structure labelled placenta, annotating it as bringing the two blood supplies close so that glucose and oxygen pass to the embryo and wastes pass back. At the uterine wall, mark development for about nine months and delivery by muscular contraction. Add a final note at the lining: if fertilisation does not occur, this lining is shed as the menstrual flow.

items.stem: Show that variation is necessary for the survival of a species, using a reasoned argument with an example.
items.answer: Consider a population of a species living in a pond at a particular temperature, and suppose first that every individual is genetically identical, as would nearly be the case in a population reproducing asexually with perfect copying. Every individual then has the same tolerance to temperature, the same susceptibility to every disease and the same requirements. Now let the conditions change: the water temperature rises sharply, or a new bacterium arrives. Whatever the change, it affects every individual in exactly the same way. If it lies within the tolerance of one individual it lies within the tolerance of all, and the population survives unharmed. But if it lies outside that tolerance it lies outside the tolerance of all, and the entire population is destroyed, taking the species with it. Uniformity therefore makes survival an all-or-nothing matter decided by a single threshold. Now suppose instead that the individuals vary, as they do in a sexually reproducing population, so that their tolerances are spread over a range. The same rise in temperature now kills many but not all: those whose tolerance happens to be higher survive, reproduce, and re-establish the population, which continues in a form better suited to the new conditions. The change has reduced the numbers without ending the lineage. The conclusion follows: since conditions do change, and since no organism can be designed in advance for a change that has not yet happened, the only protection available to a species is to contain individuals that differ. A concrete case is the heat-tolerant bacteria in a pond that is warmed: most die, a few survive and the population recovers. Variation is therefore not an imperfection in reproduction but the mechanism by which a species remains viable over time, and this is precisely why the slight inaccuracy of DNA copying, and the far greater reshuffling in sexual reproduction, are advantages rather than faults.
